summaries.example: Imagine your class invents the word “glimmerbug” for a tiny toy that lights up. That is a stipulative definition: your group gives the new word a meaning. If you point to one toy and say, “Let this be called Glimmerbug,” that is also an ostensive definition because you use something you can see. A dictionary definition works differently: it reports how people already use a word.
summaries.summary: A definition explains or sets the meaning of something. Philosophers study definitions because definitions do many different jobs. A dictionary usually describes how a word is used. A stipulative definition gives a term a meaning by choice, while a descriptive definition tries to fit meanings already in use. An explicative definition improves an older, less exact idea for a particular purpose. An ostensive definition uses pointing or experience to connect a term with something. Philosophers also distinguish asking what a word means from asking what a thing really is. These activities can overlap, so the kinds of definitions are not perfectly separate. The main lesson is that we should ask what a definition is for before deciding whether it is good.
key_ideas: Definitions can have different jobs. They may make a word clearer, report common use, or introduce a new term.
A dictionary definition and a scientific or philosophical definition are not always trying to do the same thing.
A definition may describe an old meaning, create a new meaning, or improve an idea for a special purpose.
Definitions can depend on context and experience, especially when we point to something.
Some definitions are debated because people disagree about meaning, the important features of things, or the best way to use an idea.
summaries.why_it_matters: Definitions help us understand one another, make rules clearer, and avoid talking past each other. They are especially important in science, mathematics, law, and philosophy, where a small difference in meaning can change an argument. Learning that definitions have different purposes also helps us judge them fairly: a definition meant to report everyday use should be checked differently from one designed to make an idea more precise.

important_terms.definition: Words or sentences that explain what another word, idea, or thing means.
A definition that gives a new word a meaning by agreement, without needing to match older uses.
A definition that explains a meaning people already use, such as a dictionary entry.
A definition made by pointing to, or showing, something in a situation.
The central or most important features of something.

questions_to_think_about: When you make up a secret word with a friend, are you describing a meaning or creating one?
Can pointing to a blue object always explain what “blue” means? What might the situation leave unclear?
Why might two dictionaries give different helpful explanations of the same word?
Should a definition copy every part of an old idea, or keep only the parts useful for a purpose?

summaries.example: Suppose a mathematician defines an ordered pair ⟨x,y⟩ using sets so that two pairs are identical exactly when their first components match and their second components match. This is an explicative definition: it does not preserve every feature of the everyday idea of a pair, but it preserves the feature needed for mathematical work. By contrast, defining a new predicate G by “x is greater than 3 and less than 10” can fix its use without changing what was already provable in the original language. A proposed definition containing an unaccounted-for variable may fail because it does not determine how G is to be used.
summaries.summary: The SEP entry presents definition as a family of activities rather than a single operation. A real definition seeks what a thing is, while a nominal definition concerns a term’s meaning and use. Dictionary definitions are one kind of nominal definition, but philosophical definitions usually pursue more than an informative dictionary entry. Stipulative definitions assign meaning; descriptive definitions aim to fit prior usage; and explicative definitions revise an imperfect concept to make it more useful for a purpose. Ostensive definitions use context and experience to fix a referent. These categories can overlap. In formal theories, the traditional account treats many definitions as governed by two demands: Conservativeness, so a mere stipulation does not generate new claims in the old language, and Eliminability, so claims using the new term can be related to claims in the ground language. The entry also examines conditional and implicit definitions, challenges to strict reduction, Russell’s concern about vicious circles, and revision approaches to circular definitions. The broader issue is how a definition fixes use and meaning, and what standards make it legitimate.
key_ideas: Definitions are not one uniform activity. Their aims include accuracy, clarity, precision, fairness, and usefulness in a particular theory.
Real and nominal definition distinguish investigating what a thing is from explaining how a term is used, although the distinction is not simple.
Descriptive definitions can be extensionally adequate, intensionally adequate, or adequate to a term’s sense; these are different standards.
Explication deliberately preserves central functions while changing some inherited features of a concept.
For many formal definitions, the traditional account emphasizes Conservativeness and Eliminability, along with fixing the use of the new expression.
Ostensive, conditional, implicit, and circular definitions show why not every definition behaves like a simple abbreviation.
summaries.why_it_matters: Definitions shape arguments in mathematics, science, law, and philosophy. They can clarify a debate, introduce useful conceptual tools, or change what follows from a theory. But a definition is not automatically legitimate merely because it has a familiar grammatical form. We must ask whether it fixes the intended use, preserves the right background commitments, fits prior usage when that is its goal, and serves the stated purpose. These questions also explain why disputes about meaning are often disputes about deeper ideas such as essence, concepts, and explanation.

important_terms.definition: A definition aimed at what an object or kind is, often by specifying its essence; it investigates the thing referred to.
A definition aimed at the meaning and use of a term rather than at the nature of the thing it denotes.
A definition that assigns meaning to a term without promising that the assignment matches earlier usage.
A definition intended to fit existing usage, though it can be judged by different levels of adequacy.
A proposed improvement of an imperfect concept that preserves important functions while revising some earlier uses.
A definition whose interpretation depends partly on a context of demonstration and the experience of what is presented.
The requirement that adding a definition should not allow essentially new claims in the original language.
The requirement that expressions containing a defined term can, in the relevant sense, be reduced to expressions of the earlier language.

questions_to_think_about: Is “Water is H₂O” a complete explanation of the meaning of “water,” or does it answer a different question?
When does improving a concept count as explaining its meaning, and when does it become stipulating a new meaning?
Why should a definition be prevented from proving new facts about the original vocabulary?
Can a circular definition guide use even if it does not reduce to an older, non-circular expression?
Should definitions be judged independently of context, or partly by the work they are meant to do?

summaries.example: A student council wants a rule for “late work.” One proposal says, “Late work means any assignment turned in after the deadline.” This is descriptive if it reports the school’s existing practice. The council might instead decide, “For this semester, late work means work submitted more than two days after the deadline.” That is stipulative because it sets a new rule. Or it might create a clearer policy that keeps the important purpose of the old rule but handles confusing cases, such as a school server failure. That is like an explication: it improves an older idea for a particular job.
summaries.summary: Definitions are tools for explaining, organizing, and sometimes creating meaning. The entry distinguishes real definitions, which concern what a thing is, from nominal definitions, which concern a term’s meaning and use. It then describes dictionary, stipulative, descriptive, explicative, and ostensive definitions. A dictionary gives enough information for understanding a term, but a philosophical definition usually has a more specialized goal. A stipulation assigns a meaning without being bound by earlier usage. A descriptive definition must fit established use, while an explication may keep a concept’s central purpose and revise features that make it vague or unhelpful. An ostensive definition fixes a term through a demonstration in a particular context. These kinds are not completely separate. The entry also explains that formal definitions are assessed by questions about whether they preserve the original language and whether they determine how the new term can be used.
key_ideas: The word “definition” covers several activities, and each activity may have a different standard of success.
A stipulative definition creates a meaning, while a descriptive definition is answerable to meanings already in use.
An explicative definition may preserve the important role of an older idea while changing some of its details.
Real and nominal definitions ask different questions: what is the thing, and what does the term mean?
Definitions can overlap. A dictionary entry might involve pointing, and a stipulation might happen to fit earlier usage.
Formal theories ask whether a definition fixes the new term’s use and avoids proving unrelated new claims.
summaries.why_it_matters: When people disagree, they may not disagree about facts; they may be using the same word in different ways. Knowing the kinds of definitions helps us identify that problem. It also matters when writing rules, studying science, learning mathematics, or debating philosophical ideas. A useful definition should be judged by its purpose: reporting everyday use, making a rule precise, identifying a thing, or building a theory. Asking that question can make discussions clearer without pretending that every disagreement has an easy answer.

important_terms.definition: An explanation of what a term means or how people use it, rather than a claim about the thing’s deeper nature.
An account of what something really is, sometimes understood as stating its essential features.
A definition that gives a term a meaning by decision, even if earlier speakers used the term differently.
A definition that tries to match established language use and can be criticized for fitting it poorly.
A definition that reshapes an existing idea to make it more exact or useful for a chosen purpose.
A definition that uses pointing, demonstration, context, and experience to identify what a term refers to.
The idea that a definition should not create new results about the old language simply by adding a new term.

questions_to_think_about: If a group changes the meaning of a word for a project, has it defined the old word or introduced a new use?
Can a definition be accurate but still fail to explain a word’s sense?
Why might a philosopher prefer an explicative definition to a perfectly ordinary one?
What could go wrong if a definition leaves some cases unclear?
Does pointing to an object teach the whole meaning of a word, or only help fix its reference?
